However, the actual compilation of this document is thought to have occurred between 879 and 1003 CE, based on historical analysis.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}}

Another early reference is found in the {{ill|Mon'yōki|ja|門葉記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mon'yōki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, which quotes the now-lost {{ill|Ichidōki|ja|壱道記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichidōki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (dated 869 CE), suggesting that the monk [[:en:Ennin|Ennin]] designated deities like "Ise Daimyōjin" and "Kasuga Daimyōjin" as guardians of the [[:en:Twelve Devas|Twelve Heavenly Generals]]. A definitive historical mention of Myōjin is in the [[:en:Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]] entry for 886 CE, which records "Matsuo Daimyōjin" (松尾大明神) of the [[:en:Matsunoo Taisha|Matsuo Taisha]] shrine.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=76}} By the 10th century, the usage of the title Daimyōjin was well established.

During the Heian period, deities receiving special reverence were often referred to as Myōjin or Daimyōjin. In some cases, the same deity might be called by both titles in a single source, without a clear distinction between the two.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=79-80}} Scholar {{ill|Imahori Taiichi|ja|今堀太逸|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imahori Taiichi|1=Taitsu Imahori|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11376800}} observed that deities with the divine Rank {{ill|Shin'i|ja|神位|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shin'i|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 神階|1=shinkai|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11591025}} of Senior First Rank or Junior First Rank were commonly labeled as Daimyōjin.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=79}}

With the rise of {{ill|Honji suijaku|ja|本地垂迹説|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Honji suijaku|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 本地垂迹}}, these Daimyōjin were interpreted as manifestations of Buddhist {{ill|Budda|ja|仏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Budda|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 仏陀|1=Buddha|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q7055}} appearing to save the Japanese people.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=79}} For example, the early 12th-century text {{ill|Chūkan Sen|ja|注好選|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chūkan Sen|1=Chūkan Sen|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109364361}} claimed that [[:en:The Buddha|Shakyamuni Tathāgata]] appeared as "Daisha Myōjin," and referenced a supposed passage in the {{ill|Bikekyō|ja|悲華経|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bikekyō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} stating, "After my death, during the age of the latter dharma, I will appear as a Daimyōjin to save sentient beings." In 1868, the [[:en:Shinbutsu bunri|Shinbutsu Bunri]] edict led to the removal of Buddhist-derived terminology from Shinto practice.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=73}} Although the term Myōjin was not explicitly banned, it was associated with Buddhism and saw decreased use.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=73}} However, some shrines, such as those venerating {{ill|Inari Daimyōjin|ja|稲荷大明神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inari Daimyōjin|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 稲荷神|1=Inari|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q719665}}, continue to use the title today.

{{Otheruses|The term "Myōjin" as a Shinto title|The reading "Akitsumikami" for 明神|Genzonshin (現人神)}}
'''Myōjin''' (明神) is a title used in the context of [[:en:Shinbutsu-shūgō|Shinbutsu-shūgō]], referring to deities in [[:en:Shinto|Shinto]] as seen through a Buddhist perspective.

== History ==
In ancient times, deities were often referred to using the title "Ōkami" (大神), which was sometimes prefixed to shrine names. Additionally, the term {{ill|Meishin|ja|名神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Meishin|1=myoujin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11415523}}, as mentioned in the [[:en:Shoku Nihongi|Shoku Nihongi]] (entry dated 730 CE), was used as part of the imperial court's {{ill|Shakaku|ja|社格|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shakaku|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=shrine rank|WD=Q10444029}} system. The term "Myōjin" first appeared in records in the colophon of the {{ill|Sumiyoshi Taisha Jindaiki|ja|住吉大社神代記|1=Sumiyoshi Taisha Shrine Chronicles|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sumiyoshi Taisha Jindaiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Sumiyoshi Taisha Shrine Chronicles|qq=}} (dated to 731 CE), which refers to the three deities {{ill|Sokotutsu no Mikoto|ja|底筒男命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sokotutsu no Mikoto|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 住吉三神|1=Sumiyoshi sanjin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1114013}}, {{ill|Nakatsutsu no Mikoto|ja|中筒男命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakatsutsu no Mikoto|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 住吉三神|1=Sumiyoshi sanjin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1114013}}, and {{ill|Uwatsutsu no Mikoto|ja|表筒男命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uwatsutsu no Mikoto|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 住吉三神|1=Sumiyoshi sanjin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1114013}} as "Sumiyoshi Daimyōjin" (住吉大明神). However, the actual compilation of this document is thought to have occurred between 879 and 1003 CE, based on historical analysis.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}}

Another early reference is found in the {{ill|Mon'yōki|ja|門葉記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mon'yōki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, which quotes the now-lost {{ill|Ichidōki|ja|壱道記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichidōki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (dated 869 CE), suggesting that the monk [[:en:Ennin|Ennin]] designated deities like "Ise Daimyōjin" and "Kasuga Daimyōjin" as guardians of the [[:en:Twelve Devas|Twelve Heavenly Generals]]. A definitive historical mention of Myōjin is in the [[:en:Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]] entry for 886 CE, which records "Matsuo Daimyōjin" (松尾大明神) of the [[:en:Matsunoo Taisha|Matsuo Taisha]] shrine.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=76}} By the 10th century, the usage of the title Daimyōjin was well established.

During the Heian period, deities receiving special reverence were often referred to as Myōjin or Daimyōjin. In some cases, the same deity might be called by both titles in a single source, without a clear distinction between the two.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=79-80}} Scholar {{ill|Imahori Taiichi|ja|今堀太逸|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imahori Taiichi|1=Taitsu Imahori|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11376800}} observed that deities with the divine Rank {{ill|Shin'i|ja|神位|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shin'i|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 神階|1=shinkai|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11591025}} of Senior First Rank or Junior First Rank were commonly labeled as Daimyōjin.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=79}}

With the rise of {{ill|Honji suijaku|ja|本地垂迹説|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Honji suijaku|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 本地垂迹}}, these Daimyōjin were interpreted as manifestations of Buddhist {{ill|Budda|ja|仏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Budda|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 仏陀|1=Buddha|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q7055}} appearing to save the Japanese people.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=79}} For example, the early 12th-century text {{ill|Chūkan Sen|ja|注好選|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chūkan Sen|1=Chūkan Sen|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109364361}} claimed that [[:en:The Buddha|Shakyamuni Tathāgata]] appeared as "Daisha Myōjin," and referenced a supposed passage in the {{ill|Bikekyō|ja|悲華経|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bikekyō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} stating, "After my death, during the age of the latter dharma, I will appear as a Daimyōjin to save sentient beings." While this passage is not found in the actual text of the Bikekyō, the belief became widely accepted.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=82}}

From the medieval to early modern periods, deities were rarely referred to by their original names and were instead called by titles such as Myōjin or Gongen.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}} The Yoshida Shintō school institutionalized the granting of Myōjin titles to deities.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}} In 1591, the court posthumously conferred the title "Toyokuni Daimyōjin" upon [[:en:Toyotomi Hideyoshi|Toyotomi Hideyoshi]].{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}} During the Edo period, a debate arose over the posthumous title for [[:en:Tokugawa Ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]], with [[:en:Tenkai|Tenkai]] advocating for "Daigongen" and [[:en:Ishin Sūden|Ishin Sūden]] proposing "Daimyōjin."{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}}

In 1868, the [[:en:Shinbutsu bunri|Shinbutsu Bunri]] edict led to the removal of Buddhist-derived terminology from Shinto practice.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=73}} Although the term Myōjin was not explicitly banned, it was associated with Buddhism and saw decreased use.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=73}} However, some shrines, such as those venerating {{ill|Inari Daimyōjin|ja|稲荷大明神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inari Daimyōjin|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 稲荷神|1=Inari|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q719665}}, continue to use the title today.

From the medieval to early modern periods, deities were rarely referred to by their original names and were instead called by titles such as Myōjin or Gongen.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}} The Yoshida Shintō school institutionalized the granting of Myōjin titles to deities.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}} In 1591, the court posthumously conferred the title "Toyokuni Daimyōjin" upon [[:en:Toyotomi Hideyoshi|Toyotomi Hideyoshi]].{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}} During the Edo period, a debate arose over the posthumous title for [[:en:Tokugawa Ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]], with [[:en:Tenkai|Tenkai]] advocating for "Daigongen" and [[:en:Ishin Sūden|Ishin Sūden]] proposing "Daimyōjin."{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}}

In 1868, the [[:en:Shinbutsu bunri|Shinbutsu Bunri]] edict led to the removal of Buddhist-derived terminology from Shinto practice.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=73}} Although the term Myōjin was not explicitly banned, it was associated with Buddhism and saw decreased use.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=73}} However, some shrines, such as those venerating {{ill|Inari Daimyōjin|ja|稲荷大明神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inari Daimyōjin|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 稲荷神|1=Inari|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q719665}}, continue to use the title today.

Wikidata name: Myōjin Taisha
[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 08:22, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}}
{{Otheruses|The term "Myōjin" as a Shinto title|The reading "Akitsumikami" for 明神|Genzonshin (現人神)}}
'''Myōjin''' (明神) is a title used in the context of [[:en:Shinbutsu-shūgō|Shinbutsu-shūgō]], referring to deities in [[:en:Shinto|Shinto]] as seen through a Buddhist perspective.

== History ==
In ancient times, deities were often referred to using the title "Ōkami" (大神), which was sometimes prefixed to shrine names. Additionally, the term {{ill|Meishin|ja|名神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Meishin|1=myoujin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11415523}}, as mentioned in the [[:en:Shoku Nihongi|Shoku Nihongi]] (entry dated 730 CE), was used as part of the imperial court's {{ill|Shakaku|ja|社格|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shakaku|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=shrine rank|WD=Q10444029}} system. The term "Myōjin" first appeared in records in the colophon of the {{ill|Sumiyoshi Taisha Jindaiki|ja|住吉大社神代記|1=Sumiyoshi Taisha Shrine Chronicles|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sumiyoshi Taisha Jindaiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Sumiyoshi Taisha Shrine Chronicles|qq=}} (dated to 731 CE), which refers to the three deities {{ill|Sokotutsu no Mikoto|ja|底筒男命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sokotutsu no Mikoto|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 住吉三神|1=Sumiyoshi sanjin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1114013}}, {{ill|Nakatsutsu no Mikoto|ja|中筒男命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakatsutsu no Mikoto|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 住吉三神|1=Sumiyoshi sanjin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1114013}}, and {{ill|Uwatsutsu no Mikoto|ja|表筒男命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uwatsutsu no Mikoto|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 住吉三神|1=Sumiyoshi sanjin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1114013}} as "Sumiyoshi Daimyōjin" (住吉大明神). However, the actual compilation of this document is thought to have occurred between 879 and 1003 CE, based on historical analysis.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}}

Another early reference is found in the {{ill|Mon'yōki|ja|門葉記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mon'yōki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, which quotes the now-lost {{ill|Ichidōki|ja|壱道記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichidōki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (dated 869 CE), suggesting that the monk [[:en:Ennin|Ennin]] designated deities like "Ise Daimyōjin" and "Kasuga Daimyōjin" as guardians of the [[:en:Twelve Devas|Twelve Heavenly Generals]]. A definitive historical mention of Myōjin is in the [[:en:Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]] entry for 886 CE, which records "Matsuo Daimyōjin" (松尾大明神) of the [[:en:Matsunoo Taisha|Matsuo Taisha]] shrine.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=76}} By the 10th century, the usage of the title Daimyōjin was well established.

During the Heian period, deities receiving special reverence were often referred to as Myōjin or Daimyōjin. In some cases, the same deity might be called by both titles in a single source, without a clear distinction between the two.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=79-80}} Scholar {{ill|Imahori Taiichi|ja|今堀太逸|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imahori Taiichi|1=Taitsu Imahori|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11376800}} observed that deities with the divine Rank {{ill|Shin'i|ja|神位|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shin'i|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 神階|1=shinkai|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11591025}} of Senior First Rank or Junior First Rank were commonly labeled as Daimyōjin.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=79}}

With the rise of {{ill|Honji suijaku|ja|本地垂迹説|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Honji suijaku|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 本地垂迹}}, these Daimyōjin were interpreted as manifestations of Buddhist {{ill|Budda|ja|仏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Budda|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 仏陀|1=Buddha|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q7055}} appearing to save the Japanese people.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=79}} For example, the early 12th-century text {{ill|Chūkan Sen|ja|注好選|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chūkan Sen|1=Chūkan Sen|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109364361}} claimed that [[:en:The Buddha|Shakyamuni Tathāgata]] appeared as "Daisha Myōjin," and referenced a supposed passage in the {{ill|Bikekyō|ja|悲華経|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bikekyō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} stating, "After my death, during the age of the latter dharma, I will appear as a Daimyōjin to save sentient beings." While this passage is not found in the actual text of the Bikekyō, the belief became widely accepted.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=82}}

From the medieval to early modern periods, deities were rarely referred to by their original names and were instead called by titles such as Myōjin or Gongen.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}} The Yoshida Shintō school institutionalized the granting of Myōjin titles to deities.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}} In 1591, the court posthumously conferred the title "Toyokuni Daimyōjin" upon [[:en:Toyotomi Hideyoshi|Toyotomi Hideyoshi]].{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}} During the Edo period, a debate arose over the posthumous title for [[:en:Tokugawa Ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]], with [[:en:Tenkai|Tenkai]] advocating for "Daigongen" and [[:en:Ishin Sūden|Ishin Sūden]] proposing "Daimyōjin."{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}}

In 1868, the [[:en:Shinbutsu bunri|Shinbutsu Bunri]] edict led to the removal of Buddhist-derived terminology from Shinto practice.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=73}} Although the term Myōjin was not explicitly banned, it was associated with Buddhism and saw decreased use.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=73}} However, some shrines, such as those venerating {{ill|Inari Daimyōjin|ja|稲荷大明神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inari Daimyōjin|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 稲荷神|1=Inari|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q719665}}, continue to use the title today.

{{Otheruses|The term "Myōjin" as a Shinto title|The reading "Akitsumikami" for 明神|Genzonshin (現人神)}}
'''Myōjin''' (明神) is a title used in the context of [[:en:Shinbutsu-shūgō|Shinbutsu-shūgō]], referring to deities in [[:en:Shinto|Shinto]] as seen through a Buddhist perspective.

== History ==
In ancient times, deities were often referred to using the title "Ōkami" (大神), which was sometimes prefixed to shrine names. Additionally, the term {{ill|Meishin|ja|名神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Meishin|1=myoujin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11415523}}, as mentioned in the [[:en:Shoku Nihongi|Shoku Nihongi]] (entry dated 730 CE), was used as part of the imperial court's {{ill|Shakaku|ja|社格|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shakaku|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=shrine rank|WD=Q10444029}} system. The term "Myōjin" first appeared in records in the colophon of the {{ill|Sumiyoshi Taisha Jindaiki|ja|住吉大社神代記|1=Sumiyoshi Taisha Shrine Chronicles|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sumiyoshi Taisha Jindaiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Sumiyoshi Taisha Shrine Chronicles|qq=}} (dated to 731 CE), which refers to the three deities {{ill|Sokotutsu no Mikoto|ja|底筒男命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sokotutsu no Mikoto|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 住吉三神|1=Sumiyoshi sanjin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1114013}}, {{ill|Nakatsutsu no Mikoto|ja|中筒男命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakatsutsu no Mikoto|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 住吉三神|1=Sumiyoshi sanjin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1114013}}, and {{ill|Uwatsutsu no Mikoto|ja|表筒男命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uwatsutsu no Mikoto|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 住吉三神|1=Sumiyoshi sanjin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1114013}} as "Sumiyoshi Daimyōjin" (住吉大明神). However, the actual compilation of this document is thought to have occurred between 879 and 1003 CE, based on historical analysis.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}}

Another early reference is found in the {{ill|Mon'yōki|ja|門葉記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mon'yōki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, which quotes the now-lost {{ill|Ichidōki|ja|壱道記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichidōki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (dated 869 CE), suggesting that the monk [[:en:Ennin|Ennin]] designated deities like "Ise Daimyōjin" and "Kasuga Daimyōjin" as guardians of the [[:en:Twelve Devas|Twelve Heavenly Generals]]. A definitive historical mention of Myōjin is in the [[:en:Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]] entry for 886 CE, which records "Matsuo Daimyōjin" (松尾大明神) of the [[:en:Matsunoo Taisha|Matsuo Taisha]] shrine.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=76}} By the 10th century, the usage of the title Daimyōjin was well established.

During the Heian period, deities receiving special reverence were often referred to as Myōjin or Daimyōjin. In some cases, the same deity might be called by both titles in a single source, without a clear distinction between the two.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=79-80}} Scholar {{ill|Imahori Taiichi|ja|今堀太逸|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imahori Taiichi|1=Taitsu Imahori|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11376800}} observed that deities with the divine Rank {{ill|Shin'i|ja|神位|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shin'i|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 神階|1=shinkai|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11591025}} of Senior First Rank or Junior First Rank were commonly labeled as Daimyōjin.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=79}}

With the rise of {{ill|Honji suijaku|ja|本地垂迹説|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Honji suijaku|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 本地垂迹}}, these Daimyōjin were interpreted as manifestations of Buddhist {{ill|Budda|ja|仏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Budda|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 仏陀|1=Buddha|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q7055}} appearing to save the Japanese people.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=79}} For example, the early 12th-century text {{ill|Chūkan Sen|ja|注好選|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chūkan Sen|1=Chūkan Sen|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109364361}} claimed that [[:en:The Buddha|Shakyamuni Tathāgata]] appeared as "Daisha Myōjin," and referenced a supposed passage in the {{ill|Bikekyō|ja|悲華経|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bikekyō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} stating, "After my death, during the age of the latter dharma, I will appear as a Daimyōjin to save sentient beings." While this passage is not found in the actual text of the Bikekyō, the belief became widely accepted.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=82}}

From the medieval to early modern periods, deities were rarely referred to by their original names and were instead called by titles such as Myōjin or Gongen.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}} The Yoshida Shintō school institutionalized the granting of Myōjin titles to deities.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}} In 1591, the court posthumously conferred the title "Toyokuni Daimyōjin" upon [[:en:Toyotomi Hideyoshi|Toyotomi Hideyoshi]].{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}} During the Edo period, a debate arose over the posthumous title for [[:en:Tokugawa Ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]], with [[:en:Tenkai|Tenkai]] advocating for "Daigongen" and [[:en:Ishin Sūden|Ishin Sūden]] proposing "Daimyōjin."{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}}

In 1868, the [[:en:Shinbutsu bunri|Shinbutsu Bunri]] edict led to the removal of Buddhist-derived terminology from Shinto practice.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=73}} Although the term Myōjin was not explicitly banned, it was associated with Buddhism and saw decreased use.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=73}} However, some shrines, such as those venerating {{ill|Inari Daimyōjin|ja|稲荷大明神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inari Daimyōjin|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 稲荷神|1=Inari|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q719665}}, continue to use the title today.

The term "Myōjin" first appeared in records in the colophon of the {{ill|Sumiyoshi Taisha Jindaiki|ja|住吉大社神代記|1=Sumiyoshi Taisha Shrine Chronicles|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sumiyoshi Taisha Jindaiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Sumiyoshi Taisha Shrine Chronicles|qq=}} (dated to 731 CE), which refers to the three deities {{ill|Sokotutsu no Mikoto|ja|底筒男命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sokotutsu no Mikoto|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 住吉三神|1=Sumiyoshi sanjin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1114013}}, {{ill|Nakatsutsu no Mikoto|ja|中筒男命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakatsutsu no Mikoto|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 住吉三神|1=Sumiyoshi sanjin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1114013}}, and {{ill|Uwatsutsu no Mikoto|ja|表筒男命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uwatsutsu no Mikoto|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 住吉三神|1=Sumiyoshi sanjin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1114013}} as "Sumiyoshi Daimyōjin" (住吉大明神). However, the actual compilation of this document is thought to have occurred between 879 and 1003 CE, based on historical analysis.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}}

Another early reference is found in the {{ill|Mon'yōki|ja|門葉記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mon'yōki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, which quotes the now-lost {{ill|Ichidōki|ja|壱道記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichidōki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (dated 869 CE), suggesting that the monk [[:en:Ennin|Ennin]] designated deities like "Ise Daimyōjin" and "Kasuga Daimyōjin" as guardians of the [[:en:Twelve Devas|Twelve Heavenly Generals]]. '''Myōjin''' (明神) is a title used in the context of {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|Shinbutsu-shūgō|WD=Q2279088|lt=Shinbutsu-shūgō}}, referring to deities in {{ill|Shinto|en|Shinto|WD=Q812767|lt=Shinto}} as seen through a Buddhist perspective.

== History ==
In ancient times, deities were often referred to using the title "Ōkami" (大神), which was sometimes prefixed to shrine names. Additionally, the term {{ill|Meishin|ja|名神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Meishin|1=myoujin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11415523}}, as mentioned in the {{ill|Shoku Nihongi|en|Shoku Nihongi|WD=Q611399|lt=Shoku Nihongi}} (entry dated 730 CE), was used as part of the imperial court's {{ill|Shakaku|ja|社格|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shakaku|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=shrine rank|WD=Q10444029}} system. The term "Myōjin" first appeared in records in the colophon of the {{ill|Sumiyoshi Taisha Jindaiki|ja|住吉大社神代記|1=Sumiyoshi Taisha Shrine Chronicles|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sumiyoshi Taisha Jindaiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Sumiyoshi Taisha Shrine Chronicles|qq=}} (dated to 731 CE), which refers to the three deities {{ill|Sokotutsu no Mikoto|ja|底筒男命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sokotutsu no Mikoto|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 住吉三神|1=Sumiyoshi sanjin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1114013}}, {{ill|Nakatsutsu no Mikoto|ja|中筒男命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakatsutsu no Mikoto|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 住吉三神|1=Sumiyoshi sanjin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1114013}}, and {{ill|Uwatsutsu no Mikoto|ja|表筒男命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uwatsutsu no Mikoto|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 住吉三神|1=Sumiyoshi sanjin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1114013}} as "Sumiyoshi Daimyōjin" (住吉大明神). However, the actual compilation of this document is thought to have occurred between 879 and 1003 CE, based on historical analysis.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}}

Another early reference is found in the {{ill|Mon'yōki|ja|門葉記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mon'yōki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, which quotes the now-lost {{ill|Ichidōki|ja|壱道記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichidōki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (dated 869 CE), suggesting that the monk {{ill|Ennin|en|Ennin|WD=Q732282|lt=Ennin}} designated deities like "Ise Daimyōjin" and "Kasuga Daimyōjin" as guardians of the {{ill|Twelve Devas|en|Twelve Devas|WD=Q9503981|lt=Twelve Heavenly Generals}}. A definitive historical mention of Myōjin is in the {{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|en|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|WD=Q1052981|lt=Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku}} entry for 886 CE, which records "Matsuo Daimyōjin" (松尾大明神) of the {{ill|Matsunoo Taisha|en|Matsunoo Taisha|WD=Q710302|lt=Matsuo Taisha}} shrine.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=76}} By the 10th century, the usage of the title Daimyōjin was well established.

During the Heian period, deities receiving special reverence were often referred to as Myōjin or Daimyōjin. In some cases, the same deity might be called by both titles in a single source, without a clear distinction between the two.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=79-80}} Scholar {{ill|Imahori Taiichi|ja|今堀太逸|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imahori Taiichi|1=Taitsu Imahori|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11376800}} observed that deities with the divine Rank {{ill|Shin'i|ja|神位|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shin'i|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 神階|1=shinkai|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11591025}} of Senior First Rank or Junior First Rank were commonly labeled as Daimyōjin.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=79}}

With the rise of {{ill|Honji suijaku|ja|本地垂迹説|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Honji suijaku|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 本地垂迹}}, these Daimyōjin were interpreted as manifestations of Buddhist {{ill|Budda|ja|仏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Budda|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 仏陀|1=Buddha|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q7055}} appearing to save the Japanese people.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=79}} For example, the early 12th-century text {{ill|Chūkan Sen|ja|注好選|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chūkan Sen|1=Chūkan Sen|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109364361}} claimed that {{ill|The Buddha|en|The Buddha|WD=Q9441|lt=Shakyamuni Tathāgata}} appeared as "Daisha Myōjin," and referenced a supposed passage in the {{ill|Bikekyō|ja|悲華経|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bikekyō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} stating, "After my death, during the age of the latter dharma, I will appear as a Daimyōjin to save sentient beings." While this passage is not found in the actual text of the Bikekyō, the belief became widely accepted.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=82}}

From the medieval to early modern periods, deities were rarely referred to by their original names and were instead called by titles such as Myōjin or Gongen.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}} The Yoshida Shintō school institutionalized the granting of Myōjin titles to deities.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}} In 1591, the court posthumously conferred the title "Toyokuni Daimyōjin" upon {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|en|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|WD=Q187550|lt=Toyotomi Hideyoshi}}.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}} During the Edo period, a debate arose over the posthumous title for {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|en|Tokugawa Ieyasu|WD=Q171977|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu}}, with {{ill|Tenkai|en|Tenkai|WD=Q1142310|lt=Tenkai}} advocating for "Daigongen" and {{ill|Ishin Sūden|en|Ishin Sūden|WD=Q911880|lt=Ishin Sūden}} proposing "Daimyōjin."{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}}

In 1868, the {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|en|Shinbutsu bunri|WD=Q1970535|lt=Shinbutsu Bunri}} edict led to the removal of Buddhist-derived terminology from Shinto practice.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=73}} Although the term Myōjin was not explicitly banned, it was associated with Buddhism and saw decreased use.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=73}} However, some shrines, such as those venerating {{ill|Inari Daimyōjin|ja|稲荷大明神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inari Daimyōjin|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 稲荷神|1=Inari|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q719665}}, continue to use the title today.

With the rise of {{ill|Honji suijaku|ja|本地垂迹説|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Honji suijaku|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 本地垂迹}}, these Daimyōjin were interpreted as manifestations of Buddhist {{ill|Budda|ja|仏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Budda|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 仏陀|1=Buddha|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q7055}} appearing to save the Japanese people.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=79}} For example, the early 12th-century text {{ill|Chūkan Sen|ja|注好選|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chūkan Sen|1=Chūkan Sen|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109364361}} claimed that {{ill|The Buddha|en|The Buddha|WD=Q9441|lt=Shakyamuni Tathāgata}} appeared as "Daisha Myōjin," and referenced a supposed passage in the {{ill|Bikekyō|ja|悲華経|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bikekyō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} stating, "After my death, during the age of the latter dharma, I will appear as a Daimyōjin to save sentient beings." While this passage is not found in the actual text of the Bikekyō, the belief became widely accepted.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=82}}

'''Myōjin''' (明神) is a title used in the context of {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|Shinbutsu-shūgō|WD=Q2279088|lt=Shinbutsu-shūgō}}, referring to deities in {{ill|Shinto|en|Shinto|WD=Q812767|lt=Shinto}} as seen through a Buddhist perspective.

== History ==
In ancient times, deities were often referred to using the title "Ōkami" (大神), which was sometimes prefixed to shrine names. Additionally, the term {{ill|Meishin|ja|名神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Meishin|1=myoujin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11415523}}, as mentioned in the {{ill|Shoku Nihongi|en|Shoku Nihongi|WD=Q611399|lt=Shoku Nihongi}} (entry dated 730 CE), was used as part of the imperial court's {{ill|Shakaku|ja|社格|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shakaku|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=shrine rank|WD=Q10444029}} system. The term "Myōjin" first appeared in records in the colophon of the {{ill|Sumiyoshi Taisha Jindaiki|ja|住吉大社神代記|1=Sumiyoshi Taisha Shrine Chronicles|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sumiyoshi Taisha Jindaiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Sumiyoshi Taisha Shrine Chronicles|qq=}} (dated to 731 CE), which refers to the three deities {{ill|Sokotutsu no Mikoto|ja|底筒男命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sokotutsu no Mikoto|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 住吉三神|1=Sumiyoshi sanjin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1114013}}, {{ill|Nakatsutsu no Mikoto|ja|中筒男命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakatsutsu no Mikoto|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 住吉三神|1=Sumiyoshi sanjin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1114013}}, and {{ill|Uwatsutsu no Mikoto|ja|表筒男命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uwatsutsu no Mikoto|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 住吉三神|1=Sumiyoshi sanjin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1114013}} as "Sumiyoshi Daimyōjin" (住吉大明神). However, the actual compilation of this document is thought to have occurred between 879 and 1003 CE, based on historical analysis.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}}

Another early reference is found in the {{ill|Mon'yōki|ja|門葉記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mon'yōki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, which quotes the now-lost {{ill|Ichidōki|ja|壱道記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichidōki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (dated 869 CE), suggesting that the monk {{ill|Ennin|en|Ennin|WD=Q732282|lt=Ennin}} designated deities like "Ise Daimyōjin" and "Kasuga Daimyōjin" as guardians of the {{ill|Twelve Devas|en|Twelve Devas|WD=Q9503981|lt=Twelve Heavenly Generals}}. A definitive historical mention of Myōjin is in the {{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|en|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|WD=Q1052981|lt=Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku}} entry for 886 CE, which records "Matsuo Daimyōjin" (松尾大明神) of the {{ill|Matsunoo Taisha|en|Matsunoo Taisha|WD=Q710302|lt=Matsuo Taisha}} shrine.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=76}} By the 10th century, the usage of the title Daimyōjin was well established.

During the Heian period, deities receiving special reverence were often referred to as Myōjin or Daimyōjin. In some cases, the same deity might be called by both titles in a single source, without a clear distinction between the two.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=79-80}} Scholar {{ill|Imahori Taiichi|ja|今堀太逸|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imahori Taiichi|1=Taitsu Imahori|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11376800}} observed that deities with the divine Rank {{ill|Shin'i|ja|神位|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shin'i|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 神階|1=shinkai|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11591025}} of Senior First Rank or Junior First Rank were commonly labeled as Daimyōjin.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=79}}

With the rise of {{ill|Honji suijaku|ja|本地垂迹説|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Honji suijaku|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 本地垂迹}}, these Daimyōjin were interpreted as manifestations of Buddhist {{ill|Budda|ja|仏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Budda|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 仏陀|1=Buddha|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q7055}} appearing to save the Japanese people.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=79}} For example, the early 12th-century text {{ill|Chūkan Sen|ja|注好選|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chūkan Sen|1=Chūkan Sen|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109364361}} claimed that {{ill|The Buddha|en|The Buddha|WD=Q9441|lt=Shakyamuni Tathāgata}} appeared as "Daisha Myōjin," and referenced a supposed passage in the {{ill|Bikekyō|ja|悲華経|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bikekyō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} stating, "After my death, during the age of the latter dharma, I will appear as a Daimyōjin to save sentient beings." While this passage is not found in the actual text of the Bikekyō, the belief became widely accepted.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=82}}

From the medieval to early modern periods, deities were rarely referred to by their original names and were instead called by titles such as Myōjin or Gongen.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}} The Yoshida Shintō school institutionalized the granting of Myōjin titles to deities.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}} In 1591, the court posthumously conferred the title "Toyokuni Daimyōjin" upon {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|en|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|WD=Q187550|lt=Toyotomi Hideyoshi}}.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}} During the Edo period, a debate arose over the posthumous title for {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|en|Tokugawa Ieyasu|WD=Q171977|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu}}, with {{ill|Tenkai|en|Tenkai|WD=Q1142310|lt=Tenkai}} advocating for "Daigongen" and {{ill|Ishin Sūden|en|Ishin Sūden|WD=Q911880|lt=Ishin Sūden}} proposing "Daimyōjin."{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}}

In 1868, the {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|en|Shinbutsu bunri|WD=Q1970535|lt=Shinbutsu Bunri}} edict led to the removal of Buddhist-derived terminology from Shinto practice.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=73}} Although the term Myōjin was not explicitly banned, it was associated with Buddhism and saw decreased use.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=73}} However, some shrines, such as those venerating {{ill|Inari Daimyōjin|ja|稲荷大明神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inari Daimyōjin|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 稲荷神|1=Inari|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q719665}}, continue to use the title today.

{{Otheruses|The term "Myōjin" as a Shinto title|The reading "Akitsumikami" for 明神|Genzonshin (現人神)}}
'''Myōjin''' (明神) is a title used in the context of {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|Shinbutsu-shūgō|WD=Q2279088|lt=Shinbutsu-shūgō}}, referring to deities in {{ill|Shinto|en|Shinto|WD=Q812767|lt=Shinto}} as seen through a Buddhist perspective.

== History ==
In ancient times, deities were often referred to using the title "Ōkami" (大神), which was sometimes prefixed to shrine names. Additionally, the term {{ill|Meishin|ja|名神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Meishin|1=myoujin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11415523}}, as mentioned in the {{ill|Shoku Nihongi|en|Shoku Nihongi|WD=Q611399|lt=Shoku Nihongi}} (entry dated 730 CE), was used as part of the imperial court's {{ill|Shakaku|ja|社格|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shakaku|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=shrine rank|WD=Q10444029}} system. The term "Myōjin" first appeared in records in the colophon of the {{ill|Sumiyoshi Taisha Jindaiki|ja|住吉大社神代記|1=Sumiyoshi Taisha Shrine Chronicles|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sumiyoshi Taisha Jindaiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Sumiyoshi Taisha Shrine Chronicles|qq=}} (dated to 731 CE), which refers to the three deities {{ill|Sokotutsu no Mikoto|ja|底筒男命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sokotutsu no Mikoto|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 住吉三神|1=Sumiyoshi sanjin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1114013}}, {{ill|Nakatsutsu no Mikoto|ja|中筒男命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakatsutsu no Mikoto|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 住吉三神|1=Sumiyoshi sanjin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1114013}}, and {{ill|Uwatsutsu no Mikoto|ja|表筒男命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uwatsutsu no Mikoto|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 住吉三神|1=Sumiyoshi sanjin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1114013}} as "Sumiyoshi Daimyōjin" (住吉大明神). However, the actual compilation of this document is thought to have occurred between 879 and 1003 CE, based on historical analysis.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}}

Another early reference is found in the {{ill|Mon'yōki|ja|門葉記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mon'yōki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, which quotes the now-lost {{ill|Ichidōki|ja|壱道記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichidōki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (dated 869 CE), suggesting that the monk {{ill|Ennin|en|Ennin|WD=Q732282|lt=Ennin}} designated deities like "Ise Daimyōjin" and "Kasuga Daimyōjin" as guardians of the {{ill|Twelve Devas|en|Twelve Devas|WD=Q9503981|lt=Twelve Heavenly Generals}}. A definitive historical mention of Myōjin is in the {{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|en|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|WD=Q1052981|lt=Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku}} entry for 886 CE, which records "Matsuo Daimyōjin" (松尾大明神) of the {{ill|Matsunoo Taisha|en|Matsunoo Taisha|WD=Q710302|lt=Matsuo Taisha}} shrine.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=76}} By the 10th century, the usage of the title Daimyōjin was well established.

During the Heian period, deities receiving special reverence were often referred to as Myōjin or Daimyōjin. In some cases, the same deity might be called by both titles in a single source, without a clear distinction between the two.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=79-80}} Scholar {{ill|Imahori Taiichi|ja|今堀太逸|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imahori Taiichi|1=Taitsu Imahori|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11376800}} observed that deities with the divine Rank {{ill|Shin'i|ja|神位|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shin'i|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 神階|1=shinkai|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11591025}} of Senior First Rank or Junior First Rank were commonly labeled as Daimyōjin.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=79}}

With the rise of {{ill|Honji suijaku|ja|本地垂迹説|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Honji suijaku|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 本地垂迹}}, these Daimyōjin were interpreted as manifestations of Buddhist {{ill|Budda|ja|仏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Budda|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 仏陀|1=Buddha|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q7055}} appearing to save the Japanese people.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=79}} For example, the early 12th-century text {{ill|Chūkan Sen|ja|注好選|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chūkan Sen|1=Chūkan Sen|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109364361}} claimed that {{ill|The Buddha|en|The Buddha|WD=Q9441|lt=Shakyamuni Tathāgata}} appeared as "Daisha Myōjin," and referenced a supposed passage in the {{ill|Bikekyō|ja|悲華経|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bikekyō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} stating, "After my death, during the age of the latter dharma, I will appear as a Daimyōjin to save sentient beings." While this passage is not found in the actual text of the Bikekyō, the belief became widely accepted.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=82}}

From the medieval to early modern periods, deities were rarely referred to by their original names and were instead called by titles such as Myōjin or Gongen.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}} The Yoshida Shintō school institutionalized the granting of Myōjin titles to deities.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}} In 1591, the court posthumously conferred the title "Toyokuni Daimyōjin" upon {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|en|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|WD=Q187550|lt=Toyotomi Hideyoshi}}.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}} During the Edo period, a debate arose over the posthumous title for {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|en|Tokugawa Ieyasu|WD=Q171977|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu}}, with {{ill|Tenkai|en|Tenkai|WD=Q1142310|lt=Tenkai}} advocating for "Daigongen" and {{ill|Ishin Sūden|en|Ishin Sūden|WD=Q911880|lt=Ishin Sūden}} proposing "Daimyōjin."{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}}

In 1868, the {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|en|Shinbutsu bunri|WD=Q1970535|lt=Shinbutsu Bunri}} edict led to the removal of Buddhist-derived terminology from Shinto practice.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=73}} Although the term Myōjin was not explicitly banned, it was associated with Buddhism and saw decreased use.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=73}} However, some shrines, such as those venerating {{ill|Inari Daimyōjin|ja|稲荷大明神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inari Daimyōjin|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 稲荷神|1=Inari|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q719665}}, continue to use the title today.

{{Otheruses|The term "Myōjin" as a Shinto title|The reading "Akitsumikami" for 明神|Genzonshin (現人神)}}
'''Myōjin''' (明神) is a title used in the context of {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|Shinbutsu-shūgō|WD=Q2279088|lt=Shinbutsu-shūgō|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō}}, referring to deities in {{ill|Shinto|en|Shinto|WD=Q812767|lt=Shinto|1=Shinto}} as seen through a Buddhist perspective.

== History ==
In ancient times, deities were often referred to using the title "Ōkami" (大神), which was sometimes prefixed to shrine names. Additionally, the term {{ill|Meishin|ja|名神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Meishin|1=myoujin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11415523}}, as mentioned in the {{ill|Shoku Nihongi|en|Shoku Nihongi|WD=Q611399|lt=Shoku Nihongi|1=Shoku Nihongi}} (entry dated 730 CE), was used as part of the imperial court's {{ill|Shakaku|ja|社格|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shakaku|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=Shakaku|WD=Q10444029}} system. The term "Myōjin" first appeared in records in the colophon of the {{ill|Sumiyoshi Taisha Jindaiki|ja|住吉大社神代記|1=Sumiyoshi Taisha Shrine Chronicles|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sumiyoshi Taisha Jindaiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Sumiyoshi Taisha Shrine Chronicles|qq=}} (dated to 731 CE), which refers to the three deities {{ill|Sokotutsu no Mikoto|ja|底筒男命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sokotutsu no Mikoto|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 住吉三神|1=Sumiyoshi sanjin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1114013}}, {{ill|Nakatsutsu no Mikoto|ja|中筒男命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakatsutsu no Mikoto|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 住吉三神|1=Sumiyoshi sanjin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1114013}}, and {{ill|Uwatsutsu no Mikoto|ja|表筒男命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uwatsutsu no Mikoto|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 住吉三神|1=Sumiyoshi sanjin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1114013}} as "Sumiyoshi Daimyōjin" (住吉大明神). However, the actual compilation of this document is thought to have occurred between 879 and 1003 CE, based on historical analysis.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}}

Another early reference is found in the {{ill|Mon'yōki|ja|門葉記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mon'yōki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, which quotes the now-lost {{ill|Ichidōki|ja|壱道記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichidōki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (dated 869 CE), suggesting that the monk {{ill|Ennin|en|Ennin|WD=Q732282|lt=Ennin|1=Ennin}} designated deities like "Ise Daimyōjin" and "Kasuga Daimyōjin" as guardians of the {{ill|Twelve Devas|en|Twelve Devas|WD=Q9503981|lt=Twelve Heavenly Generals|1=Jūniten}}. A definitive historical mention of Myōjin is in the {{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|en|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|WD=Q1052981|lt=Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|1=Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku}} entry for 886 CE, which records "Matsuo Daimyōjin" (松尾大明神) of the {{ill|Matsunoo Taisha|en|Matsunoo Taisha|WD=Q710302|lt=Matsuo Taisha|1=Matsunoo Taisha}} shrine.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=76}} By the 10th century, the usage of the title Daimyōjin was well established.

During the Heian period, deities receiving special reverence were often referred to as Myōjin or Daimyōjin. In some cases, the same deity might be called by both titles in a single source, without a clear distinction between the two.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=79-80}} Scholar {{ill|Imahori Taiichi|ja|今堀太逸|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imahori Taiichi|1=Taitsu Imahori|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11376800}} observed that deities with the divine Rank {{ill|Shin'i|ja|神位|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shin'i|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 神階|1=Shinkai (divine rank)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11591025}} of Senior First Rank or Junior First Rank were commonly labeled as Daimyōjin.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=79}}

With the rise of {{ill|Honji suijaku|ja|本地垂迹説|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Honji suijaku|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 本地垂迹}}, these Daimyōjin were interpreted as manifestations of Buddhist {{ill|Budda|ja|仏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Budda|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 仏陀|1=Buddha (title)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q7055}} appearing to save the Japanese people.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=79}} For example, the early 12th-century text {{ill|Chūkan Sen|ja|注好選|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chūkan Sen|1=Q109364361|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109364361}} claimed that {{ill|The Buddha|en|The Buddha|WD=Q9441|lt=Shakyamuni Tathāgata|1=The Buddha}} appeared as "Daisha Myōjin," and referenced a supposed passage in the {{ill|Bikekyō|ja|悲華経|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bikekyō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} stating, "After my death, during the age of the latter dharma, I will appear as a Daimyōjin to save sentient beings." While this passage is not found in the actual text of the Bikekyō, the belief became widely accepted.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=82}}

From the medieval to early modern periods, deities were rarely referred to by their original names and were instead called by titles such as Myōjin or Gongen.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}} The Yoshida Shintō school institutionalized the granting of Myōjin titles to deities.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}} In 1591, the court posthumously conferred the title "Toyokuni Daimyōjin" upon {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|en|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|WD=Q187550|lt=Toyotomi Hideyoshi|1=Toyotomi Hideyoshi}}.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}} During the Edo period, a debate arose over the posthumous title for {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|en|Tokugawa Ieyasu|WD=Q171977|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu|1=Tokugawa Ieyasu}}, with {{ill|Tenkai|en|Tenkai|WD=Q1142310|lt=Tenkai|1=Tenkai}} advocating for "Daigongen" and {{ill|Ishin Sūden|en|Ishin Sūden|WD=Q911880|lt=Ishin Sūden|1=Ishin Sūden}} proposing "Daimyōjin."{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=74}}

In 1868, the {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|en|Shinbutsu bunri|WD=Q1970535|lt=Shinbutsu Bunri|1=Shinbutsu bunri}} edict led to the removal of Buddhist-derived terminology from Shinto practice.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=73}} Although the term Myōjin was not explicitly banned, it was associated with Buddhism and saw decreased use.{{sfn|Nakamura Kazuharu|2009|pp=73}} However, some shrines, such as those venerating {{ill|Inari Daimyōjin|ja|稲荷大明神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inari Daimyōjin|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 稲荷神|1=Inari Ōkami|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q719665}}, continue to use the title today.
